feedback: If you predicted the total would change, compare your prediction with what you counted — turning the array does not add or take away any objects, so the total must stay the same.
Strong answer: 'It's the same counters turned on their side, so there are still 12.' That reasons from the array, not just from working both sums out.
If a learner only says 'I worked them both out', push for the structural reason: show them the rotation so commutativity is seen, not just checked.
activities.intendedInsight: The same set of objects, read in two directions, gives the same product, so multiplication can be done in either order — this is predicted and then seen by rotating, not merely stated as a rule.
learnerActions: Build an array of 3 rows of 4 counters (or dots) and count the total: 12.
Before you turn the array, predict whether the total will change if you turn it, and give your reason.
Rotate the whole array a quarter turn so it becomes 4 rows of 3 — do not add or remove any counters.
Count again and confirm the total is still 12; record 3×4 = 4×3.
Repeat with another pair you choose (e.g. 2×5 and 5×2) and state the matching fact.
Explain in your own words WHY the total cannot change when you turn the array.
activities.title: Predict then rotate the array to prove 3×4 = 4×3

feedback: If a learner recomputes the partner fact, remind them the array proof means the answer must be identical — they already know it.
Encourage them to point to the diagonal mirror on the square to justify why the facts pair up.
Note the facts that sit on the diagonal (like 3×3) have no separate partner, which is why commutativity nearly halves, rather than exactly halves, the facts to learn.
activities.intendedInsight: Because order doesn't matter for multiplication, each known fact gives its partner free, nearly halving the facts to learn, and you can pick the easier order or check your work.
learnerActions: Given a known fact (e.g. 3×8 = 24), state its commuted partner (8×3 = 24) without recomputing.
Look at a multiplication square and find the diagonal line of symmetry; notice that facts on either side of it mirror each other.
Decide which of a pair is easier to work out (e.g. 2×9 vs 9×2) and explain why using the easier order helps.
Use 'compute both ways and compare' to check one of your own answers.
activities.title: Use commutativity to get facts for free

feedback: If a learner says 12÷3 = 3÷12 'because order doesn't matter in maths', have them physically share both ways; the different outcomes make the difference felt.
Good distinction: '12÷3 gives 4, but 3÷12 gives less than one — division can't be turned round.'
Note that subtraction also does not commute (8−3 ≠ 3−8), so 'order never matters' is the mistaken rule to avoid.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplication's array can be turned freely without changing the total, but swapping the two numbers in a division (or subtraction) usually changes the answer (it only stays the same when the two numbers are equal) — so the swapping shortcut has a precise stopping point.
learnerActions: Act out 12 ÷ 3 with counters: share 12 counters into 3 equal groups and count one group (4).
Now act out 3 ÷ 12: try to share 3 counters among 12 — you cannot give everyone a whole counter, so each would get less than one.
Compare the two results and state clearly that 12÷3 ≠ 3÷12 (4 is not the same as less than one).
Try to 'rotate' the sharing the way you rotated a multiplication array, and describe why it does not work.
Decide for each pair whether order can swap: sort statements (mixing × and ÷) into 'order can swap' and 'order matters'.
Consider whether swapping works for subtraction too (e.g. 8−3 vs 3−8) and say what you find.
activities.title: Test the boundary: division does not swap

feedback: If a learner thinks the stories must be identical because the totals match, point to the different group sizes — 3 bags of 4 is a different arrangement from 4 bags of 3.
If a learner thinks the totals differ because the stories differ, have them count both to 12.
activities.intendedInsight: Different real situations can share the same product; 'same answer' is not the same as 'same story'.
learnerActions: Draw or set out '3 bags of 4' and '4 bags of 3' as two separate situations.
Confirm both give 12, then explain how the stories differ even though the answer is the same.
Match a context picture to the fact it shows, and to its commuted partner.
activities.title: Same product, different story

feedback: A convincing refutation does the sharing: 12 shared into 3 is 4 each, but 3 shared among 12 is less than one.
If the learner just says 'no' without evidence, ask them to show it with counters.
activities.intendedInsight: You can justify and defend the boundary of commutativity by producing a worked counterexample, not just asserting it.
learnerActions: Listen to a character claim 'division works both ways, like multiplication — 12÷3 is the same as 3÷12'.
Disagree and give a counterexample, backing it up by sharing counters both ways.
State the correct rule: multiplication can be swapped, division cannot.
activities.title: Refute the character who says division swaps too
